titulo: Module 01 — Exam: the certification exam, the Messages API, and the request surface

questoes.pergunta: A fintech has a support agent (Agent SDK) that can call process_refund. The policy says refunds above $500 require human approval. In an audit, 3% of the refunds above the limit were processed without approval, despite an ALL-CAPS instruction in the system prompt. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Rewrite the instruction with few-shot examples of denied refunds
Add a second model that reviews each refund and vetoes those that violate the policy before execution
Block process_refund above $500 with a hook in code
Reduce the agent's number of tools so it pays more attention to the rule
questoes.explicacao: A rule with financial consequences requires deterministic enforcement. A prompt (even with few-shot) has a nonzero failure rate.
feedbacks: Tempting because few-shot improves adherence, but it is still probabilistic: it reduces the 3%, it doesn't eliminate it.
Tempting because it looks like a 'double check', but it is more complex and also probabilistic; the tiebreaker favors deterministic code.
Correct: a hook/validation enforces the rule in 100% of cases.
Too many tools is a real anti-pattern, but it isn't the cause here; the critical rule lives only in the prompt.

questoes.pergunta: In a manual tool loop, the team ends the iteration when the response contains any text block. Users report that the agent sometimes says 'Let me look up your order' and stops without looking anything up. What is the fix?
opcoes: Decide based on stop_reason: continue on tool_use, stop on end_turn
Stop only when the text contains the word 'done'
Instruct the model in the system prompt never to write text before calling tools
Cap the loop at 5 iterations and stop when the cap is reached
questoes.explicacao: content can mix text and tool_use; the end is signaled by stop_reason, not by the presence of text.
feedbacks: Correct: stop_reason is the loop's control signal.
Anti-pattern #1: parsing natural language to decide when to stop; fragile and prone to false positives.
Attacks the symptom from the wrong side: text before tool_use is valid; the bug is in the stopping criterion.
Anti-pattern #2: an iteration cap as the primary mechanism; it only serves as a backstop.

questoes.pergunta: A research agent receives responses with 3 parallel tool_use blocks. The code executes each tool and sends each tool_result in a separate user message, each followed by a new API call. The team notices validation errors and that the model has stopped requesting tools in parallel. What should they do?
opcoes: Disable parallel use with disable_parallel_tool_use, to receive one tool at a time and avoid the error
Execute the tools sequentially and call the API after each one
Concatenate the three results into a single text block
A single user message with the three tool_result blocks, each with its tool_use_id
questoes.explicacao: All the tool_result blocks for a response go together in a single user message, each referencing the exact tool_use_id.
feedbacks: Hides the problem and loses the benefit of parallelism; it's the response protocol that is wrong.
Same protocol error, just slower: there are pending tool_use blocks without results.
Loses the tool_use_id linkage; loose text doesn't close the pending tool_use blocks.
Correct: one user message with all the results.

questoes.pergunta: In an extraction system, the fetch_document tool sometimes times out. In those cases, the code simply doesn't return a tool_result and resends the conversation. The model starts 'making up' the document's content. What is the BEST fix?
opcoes: Return an empty tool_result, without indicating an error, so as not to confuse the model
Return the tool_result with is_error: true and the cause of the error (timeout, retryable)
Instruct the model never to make up content
Remove the fetch_document tool and send the documents in the system prompt
questoes.explicacao: A tool failure should come back as a tool_result with is_error: true and context, so the model can reason about recovery.
feedbacks: Anti-pattern #7: empty-as-success hides the fact that the lookup never even ran.
Correct: an explicit, informative error.
An instruction doesn't fix the missing information; the model doesn't even know there was a failure.
A disproportionate architectural change; the problem is only the error handling.

questoes.pergunta: Structured Data Extraction scenario: on contracts of 80+ pages, the output JSON arrives cut off in the middle of a field. On short contracts everything works. What should you check FIRST?
opcoes: Whether stop_reason is max_tokens and the output limit is insufficient
Whether the model is capable of generating valid JSON
Whether the temperature is too high
Whether the system prompt asks for the JSON clearly
questoes.explicacao: Output cut off at the end, only on long documents, points to truncation by max_tokens.
feedbacks: Correct: the pattern 'only on long ones, cut off at the end' is max_tokens.
It works on the short ones, so capability isn't the problem.
Temperature doesn't cause truncation (and it is rejected on the newer models).
It works on the short ones with the same prompt; it isn't a clarity issue.

questoes.pergunta: A moderation pipeline processes user-submitted texts. In some cases the API returns HTTP 200, but content doesn't contain the expected classification and the pipeline records 'no violation'. What is the likely cause and the fix?
opcoes: Intermittent network timeout; add retry with exponential backoff and jitter
Ambiguous prompt; add few-shot
Refusal: check stop_reason == refusal before reading content
Low max_tokens; raise the limit
questoes.explicacao: A refusal arrives with HTTP 200 and stop_reason refusal; code that ignores stop_reason treats it as an empty success.
feedbacks: A timeout doesn't come back as HTTP 200.
Few-shot doesn't change the fact that the pipeline records a result without checking why generation stopped.
Correct: check stop_reason before consuming content.
Truncation would leave partial output, not missing output; and the symptom 'HTTP 200 with no useful content' points to refusal.

questoes.pergunta: An internal chatbot calls the Messages API sending, on each turn, only the user's latest message plus the system prompt. Users complain that the bot 'forgets' what was said two turns earlier. What is the explanation?
opcoes: The model's context window is too small
Prompt caching is invalidating the history
The system prompt should instruct the model to remember and summarize the conversation every turn
Stateless API: the history must be resent on every call
questoes.explicacao: The Messages API doesn't keep state; the client resends the history in messages on every call.
feedbacks: Two turns fit easily in any window; the problem is not sending them.
Caching neither stores nor deletes history; it only reuses prefixes that were sent.
An instruction doesn't bring back what wasn't sent.
Correct: stateless.

questoes.pergunta: In a support agent, the team sees in usage that input_tokens grows with every turn of the same conversation, even when the user sends short messages. What does this indicate?
opcoes: A bug in the SDK that duplicates messages
Expected behavior: the entire history is resent and billed every turn
The model is generating hidden thinking that is counted as input
The system prompt is being recompiled every turn
questoes.explicacao: Because the API is stateless, each turn resends (and bills) the accumulated history; caching and context management (Module 10) mitigate this.
feedbacks: It isn't a bug; it's a consequence of the stateless model.
Correct: resent history = growing input.
Thinking is output, not input for that turn.
There is no 'recompilation'; the system prompt is just part of the resent input.

questoes.pergunta: An insurance company needs to extract 6 fields from each claim form (one document at a time, no external tools). An architect proposes an agent built with the Agent SDK and subagents. What is the BEST approach?
opcoes: Managed Agents, so nothing has to be hosted and each session gets a sandbox
Agent SDK with one subagent per field
One call per document, with structured output
Tool Runner with one tool per field
questoes.explicacao: Extracting from a single document is a one-call task. Agents are for multi-step, open-ended work; the simplest solution wins.
feedbacks: Managed infrastructure doesn't justify an agent where a single call is enough.
Disproportionate complexity (and too many tools/subagents) for an extraction.
Correct: one call + schema.
An unnecessary tool loop; there is no external action to perform.

questoes.pergunta: A platform team wants an agent that navigates the repository (reading, editing, running commands), with audit hooks and subagents, running on the team's own CI infrastructure. Which way of building it requires the least custom code?
opcoes: Claude Agent SDK
A manual loop on the Messages API reimplementing Read/Edit/Bash
Tool Runner with custom file tools
A single call with the entire repository in the prompt
questoes.explicacao: The Agent SDK is the Claude Code harness as a library: built-in tools, hooks, subagents, and permissions, hosted by you.
feedbacks: Correct: batteries included, on your infrastructure.
Possible, but it reimplements what the Agent SDK already provides; more code, more risk.
Tool Runner has no built-in tools, hooks, or subagents; you would write all of it.
It doesn't fit/wastes context, and it can't edit files or run commands.

questoes.pergunta: A startup with no infrastructure team wants long-running agents, each session with its own isolated environment for running code and manipulating files, and versioned agent configurations. Which option?
opcoes: Tool Runner hosted on its own server
Managed Agents
A manual loop with Docker containers managed by the team
Batch API
questoes.explicacao: Managed Agents is the only option in which Anthropic runs the loop AND hosts the per-session sandbox.
feedbacks: Tool Runner is just the loop; hosting and the sandbox stay with the startup.
Correct: hosted loop + sandbox, versioned configs.
It requires exactly the infrastructure the startup doesn't have.
Batch is asynchronous bulk processing, with no multi-turn tool loop.

questoes.pergunta: A .NET service exposes 3 internal functions (check inventory, reserve item, cancel reservation) and wants Claude to use them in a loop until the order is complete. The team doesn't want to write the loop and doesn't need built-in tools or a sandbox. Which option?
opcoes: Claude Agent SDK
Managed Agents
A single call with a forced tool_choice
The API SDK's Tool Runner
questoes.explicacao: Tool Runner runs the request → execute → repeat loop for your tools, on your infrastructure.
feedbacks: Brings a full harness (built-in tools, permissions) the team doesn't need.
Adds hosting/sandbox the case doesn't call for.
A single call doesn't cover the multi-step loop; and forcing a tool returns 400 on newer models.
Correct: the simplest option that does the job.

questoes.pergunta: CI scenario: after migrating a review job to a newer model, every call started returning 400. The request uses thinking: {type: enabled, budget_tokens: 12000}. What is the fix?
opcoes: thinking: {type: adaptive} + output_config.effort
Lower budget_tokens to below max_tokens
Revert to the old model permanently
Move budget_tokens into output_config, where the new parameters live
questoes.explicacao: On the newer models, budget_tokens is rejected; adaptive thinking + effort is the current surface.
feedbacks: Correct.
That was the old rule; on the newer models the parameter itself is rejected.
Avoids the problem without solving it; the migration is feasible by adjusting the request.
There is no budget_tokens in output_config; what lives there is effort.

questoes.pergunta: Structured Data Extraction scenario: the pipeline ended messages with an assistant message containing '{' to force JSON. After the model migration, the calls fail with 400. What is the BEST replacement?
opcoes: Change the prefill to '```json'
Remove the prefill and ask to 'respond only with JSON' in the last user turn, with no other changes
Use structured outputs (output_config.format with a JSON schema)
Force a tool via tool_choice: {type: any}
questoes.explicacao: Prefill is rejected on the newer models; structured outputs guarantees conformance to the schema.
feedbacks: It's still a prefill: same 400.
An instruction helps, but it doesn't guarantee the schema in an extraction pipeline; there is a better option.
Correct: a structural guarantee.
Forcing a tool with any also returns 400 on newer models.

questoes.pergunta: A ticket classifier assigns inconsistent labels to similar cases. A developer proposes setting temperature: 0 and a low top_p on the new model. What is the correct assessment?
opcoes: Correct: zero temperature makes the model deterministic
Correct, as long as top_k: 1 is also used
Partially correct: it works if combined with a prefill of an initial label in the response
Inadequate: they are rejected on newer models; explicit criteria are missing
questoes.explicacao: Sampling parameters are rejected on the newer models and attack the wrong symptom; the inconsistency comes from vague criteria.
feedbacks: A common myth; besides, the parameter returns 400 on newer models.
top_k is also rejected on newer models.
Prefill is also rejected; it stacks two invalid parameters.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: A company runs 2 million simple classifications per day on a top-tier model with high effort. Costs have exploded, and the team wants to switch to a smaller model. What should they do BEFORE that?
opcoes: Switch straight to the smaller model, since the task is simple
Measure the same model with lower effort on a real sample
Add a routing classifier that sends easy cases to the smaller model and hard ones to the larger one
Increase max_tokens to reduce retries
questoes.explicacao: effort is the first cost × quality knob; measuring before changing anything is one of the exam's tiebreaker rules.
feedbacks: It might even work, but it skips measurement and the simplest knob.
Correct: measure the simplest knob first.
More complex than necessary before testing effort.
It doesn't reduce cost; a simple classification doesn't come anywhere near the limit.

questoes.pergunta: After migrating a code-analysis assistant to a newer model without changing the request, the team notices shallower responses on hard tasks. There are no errors. What is the most likely cause, and the action?
opcoes: The effort default changed; set it explicitly and recalibrate
The new model is less capable; revert to the old one
The new model's context window shrank; split the files into smaller parts
A high temperature was missing for 'creativity'
questoes.explicacao: Defaults (such as the effort default) can change from model to model; when migrating, set them explicitly and recalibrate.
feedbacks: Correct.
A hasty conclusion without checking the configuration.
Nothing points to a context window problem; responses come back complete, just shallow.
Sampling parameters are rejected on newer models and don't control depth.

questoes.pergunta: You are reviewing an agent's manual loop. Which TWO practices are correct? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: End the loop when the response has more text than tool_use blocks
End the loop when stop_reason is end_turn
Use the iteration cap as the primary termination criterion
When several tool_use blocks arrive, execute all of them and return all the tool_result blocks in a single user message
Discard tool_use blocks whose result failed, so as not to pollute the context
questoes.explicacao: stop_reason decides when to stop; parallel results come back together, including failures (with is_error: true).
feedbacks: Counting text is a variant of anti-pattern #1.
Correct.
Anti-pattern #2: a cap only as a backstop.
Correct.
Anti-pattern #7: a failure should come back with is_error: true.

questoes.pergunta: A team is about to migrate its extraction pipeline to a new model. Which TWO actions are the most appropriate? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Run a set of real requests against the new model to validate the request shape before deploying
Keep temperature: 0 to preserve consistency
Swap the model ID in production on a Friday and monitor over the weekend
Increase budget_tokens to compensate for reasoning changes
Review parameters the new model rejects (prefill, sampling, budget_tokens) and recalibrate effort
questoes.explicacao: Accepted parameters change from model to model; test the request shape and recalibrate effort.
feedbacks: Correct.
temperature is rejected on newer models.
Discovering a 400 in production is exactly what you want to avoid.
budget_tokens is rejected on newer models.
Correct.

questoes.pergunta: An architect proposes these rules for when the support agent should escalate to a human. Which TWO are classic exam anti-patterns? (Choose TWO.)
opcoes: Escalate when the customer explicitly asks for a human
Escalate when the request falls into a policy exception that isn't covered
Escalate when the model reports confidence below 70%
Escalate when the customer's sentiment is very negative
Escalate when there is no progress after reasonable attempts
questoes.explicacao: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated (anti-pattern #4), and sentiment ≠ complexity (anti-pattern #5). The others are legitimate triggers (Module 11).
feedbacks: Legitimate trigger: an explicit request for a human.
Legitimate trigger: a policy gap/exception.
Anti-pattern #4: self-reported confidence.
Anti-pattern #5: an angry customer with a simple problem should have it resolved.
Legitimate trigger: no progress after reasonable attempts.
